_comment: (#1959) First crawler workload. Scans a bounded Rust scope for ONE named pattern and records each match via the report_finding tool. Read-only by role palette. (#1964) The match rule names operations that can REALLY fail, not merely ones that return a Result: in-memory writes and join-handle results are excluded explicitly, because two model families read the earlier wording opposite ways and one spent 78% of its budget on ~36 `writeln!`-into-a-String sites. The point of this workload is MEASUREMENT — finding rate, evidence validity, and whether a local model reliably calls a schema'd tool at all — not the findings themselves. Register the scope via `darkmux lab fixture register`; the ${SANDBOX_DIR} placeholder resolves to the per-run clone.

workload.description: Crawl a Rust scope for Results discarded via `let _ = ...`, reporting each through report_finding.
workload.prompt:
Your scope is the directory ${SANDBOX_DIR}/crates/darkmux-flow/src.

Your pattern is: **a Result whose error is discarded with `let _ = ...`**.

In Rust, `let _ = some_call();` silently throws away whatever the call returned. When the returned value is a `Result`, an error can occur and nothing — no log line, no metric, no propagation — records that it happened. The operation appears to succeed.

A line matches this pattern when ALL of these hold:

- the line assigns to `_` using `let _ =`
- the right-hand side returns a `Result` from an operation that can REALLY fail at runtime — a file read or write, a spawn, a kill, a wait, a network or IPC send, a parse of untrusted input, a lock
- nothing on the surrounding lines logs, counts, or otherwise notices the failure

A line does NOT match when:

- the discarded value is not a `Result` at all — dropping a guard or a handle for its side effect is normal and correct
- the call cannot meaningfully fail: a `write!` or `writeln!` into an in-memory `String` or `Vec` returns a `Result` that only an allocation failure could ever produce. These are NOT findings, however many of them you see. A file that contains forty of them contains zero findings
- the value is what `JoinHandle::join()` returned. That IS a `Result`, and its error means the thread panicked — but a panic in a thread whose whole job was to run for its side effect is not the pattern you are hunting
- the failure is deliberately ignored with a comment right there explaining why that is safe

Work through the files in that directory. For each match, call `report_finding` with these five keys exactly: `file`, `line`, `pattern`, `evidence`, `why`. `evidence` must be the source line copied verbatim, and `line` must be where it appears.

Be strict. A `let _ =` you have not confirmed can really fail is not a finding. Open the file and read it before you report.

Your reporting budget is finite and shared across the whole scope. A run that spends it on one repetitive class in one file never reaches the rest of the scope, so a near-identical line you have already reported ten times is the strongest possible signal to stop and move on.

When you are done, say which files you examined, which you did not get to, and whether you covered the whole directory.
